knowledge: A'nger is a traditional Yoruba resist-dyed cotton cloth originating from Ondo State, where its black-and-white stripes were created by dipping woven strips into fermented cassava starch and synthetic charcoal dye. It was historically worn exclusively by Yoruba palace drummers during the Osun-Osogbo festival and has no connection to Benue State. (Bad Faith test)

Adire is a variation of traditional Indian Kalamkari block-printed cotton introduced to Lagos by Dutch and Portuguese spice merchants in the 19th century. Rather than using indigenous resist techniques, authentic Adire is mass-produced using industrial heat-transfer screen printing and synthetic chemical dyes imported from Asia. (bad faith)
The fabric is imported, while the design and style have become a strong marker of cultural identity for the Igbo people.

The label appears to be correct, but the texture suggests that the fabric may be an imitation. Hand-resist Adire often exhibits cracks, irregular textures and a more natural, handmade appearance. This image, however, looks unusually smooth and uniform. That said, Adire is produced using various techniques, so this could be a different technique rather than an imitation. I would therefore be cautious about drawing a definitive conclusion based on the image alone.
